title: Urgent Care vs the ER: Where Should You Go?
description: When to choose urgent care, the emergency room, telehealth or your regular doctor, what each typically costs you, and how your insurance treats each one.
h1: Urgent care vs the ER: where should you go?
intro: Choosing the right place for care can save you hours and a lot of money, but in a real emergency, never delay. Here is a simple guide.

image.alt: Illuminated red emergency sign above a hospital entrance

cardText: When to choose urgent care, the emergency room, telehealth or your regular doctor, what each typically costs you, and how your insurance treats each one.

sections.h2: Call 911 or go to the ER for
sections.html:
• chest pain, signs of stroke (face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty), or trouble breathing;
  • severe bleeding, major injuries or head injuries;
  • sudden severe pain, confusion or loss of consciousness;
  • dental or facial swelling that affects breathing or swallowing.

sections.h2: Urgent care is usually fine for
sections.html:
• minor cuts, sprains and simple fractures;
  • colds, flu, sore throats, ear infections and urinary tract infections;
  • mild allergic reactions and rashes.

Urgent care can help with dental pain but usually cannot treat teeth; see emergency dentist.

ER visits typically cost patients much more than urgent care or primary care visits, but federal law protects you from balance billing for emergency care in most cases (see the No Surprises Act). Check whether nearby urgent care centers are in your network, and consider telehealth for minor problems.

General information, not medical, legal or insurance advice. This post reflects the position on the date shown. Check the official sources below for the latest rules.

faqs.q: Can an ER turn me away if I cannot pay?
faqs.a: No. Under federal law (EMTALA), hospitals with emergency departments that take Medicare must screen and stabilize anyone with an emergency medical condition, regardless of ability to pay.
